topics.name: Classification of Solids and Intrinsic/Extrinsic Semiconductors: p-type and n-type
topics.summary: Solids are classified by their energy bands. In a conductor the valence and conduction bands overlap, so electrons move freely. An insulator has a large gap (more than 3 eV), so almost no electrons can cross it. A semiconductor has a small gap: about 1.1 eV for silicon and 0.7 eV for germanium. In a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor, heat lifts some electrons into the conduction band, each leaving a hole, so \( n_e=n_h=n_i \). Because heating creates more carriers, a semiconductor's conductivity rises with temperature, the opposite of a metal. Doping makes an extrinsic semiconductor. A pentavalent impurity (phosphorus, arsenic) donates a free electron, giving n-type material where electrons are the majority carriers and holes the minority. A trivalent impurity (boron, indium, gallium) creates a hole, giving p-type material where holes are the majority carriers and electrons the minority. Every doped crystal stays electrically neutral. The mass-action law \( n_en_h=n_i^2 \) links the two carrier concentrations.
key_formulas: n-type: \( n_e\approx N_D \); p-type: \( n_h\approx N_A \)
Band gaps: Si about 1.1 eV, Ge about 0.7 eV, insulator more than 3 eV
topics.worked_example:
Silicon with \( n_i=1.5\times10^{16}\,\text{m}^{-3} \) is doped so that \( n_e=10^{22}\,\text{m}^{-3} \). Find the hole concentration.

\( n_h=n_i^2/n_e=2.25\times10^{32}/10^{22}=2.25\times10^{10}\,\text{m}^{-3} \). Holes are the minority carriers, as expected in n-type material.
common_mistakes: Linking pentavalent impurities to p-type material or trivalent impurities to n-type material
Swapping which carrier is the majority in n-type or p-type material
Thinking a semiconductor's conductivity falls with temperature, as a metal's does
Giving a semiconductor an insulator-sized band gap of more than 3 eV
Believing an n-type crystal is negatively charged

topics.name: p-n Junction Diode: Depletion Region, Barrier Potential, and Forward/Reverse Bias
topics.summary: When p-type and n-type regions meet, majority carriers diffuse across the junction and recombine. This leaves fixed negative acceptor ions on the p-side and fixed positive donor ions on the n-side, forming a depletion region that has almost no free carriers. The ions set up a field from the n-side to the p-side and a barrier potential of about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium. At equilibrium, diffusion and drift currents cancel. In forward bias (p-side to the positive terminal) the applied voltage opposes the barrier, the depletion region narrows, and a large majority-carrier diffusion current flows once the knee voltage is passed, so the resistance is low. In reverse bias (p-side to the negative terminal) the barrier rises, the depletion region widens, and only a tiny minority-carrier drift current flows, so the resistance is very high. This reverse current is almost independent of reverse voltage but rises strongly with temperature, because minority carriers are thermally generated. A large enough reverse voltage causes breakdown.
key_formulas: Barrier potential: Si about 0.7 V, Ge about 0.3 V
Forward bias: effective barrier \( =V_0-V \); reverse bias: \( V_0+V \)
topics.worked_example:
A silicon diode (0.7 V) in forward bias is in series with 1 k\( \Omega \) across 5.7 V. Find the current.

Voltage across the resistor \( =5.7-0.7=5.0 \) V, so \( I=5.0/1000=5 \) mA. Reversing the diode gives practically zero current.
common_mistakes: Thinking forward bias widens the depletion region or reverse bias narrows it
Believing the reverse current grows strongly with reverse voltage below breakdown
Forgetting the strong temperature dependence of reverse current
Attributing reverse current to majority carriers instead of minority carriers
Confusing the barrier potential with the band gap

topics.name: Diode Applications: Rectifiers, and Zener, LED, Photodiode, and Solar Cell Devices
topics.summary: A diode's one-way conduction makes it a rectifier. A half-wave rectifier uses one diode and passes only one half-cycle, so its ripple frequency equals the input frequency. A full-wave rectifier, either centre-tap (two diodes) or bridge (four diodes), uses both half-cycles, so its ripple frequency is double the input frequency. A Zener diode is heavily doped, giving a thin depletion region and a sharp, safe breakdown. It is deliberately operated in reverse breakdown, where its voltage stays nearly constant, so it works as a voltage regulator with a series resistor. An ordinary diode is not suitable for this. An LED is forward biased; recombination releases photons of energy about equal to the band gap, so \( \lambda=hc/E_g \). A photodiode is reverse biased; light with \( h\nu>E_g \) creates electron-hole pairs, which increase the small reverse current noticeably. A solar cell needs no bias: light creates pairs that the junction field separates, producing an EMF. Band gaps near 1.5 eV suit solar cells.
key_formulas: Half-wave ripple frequency \( =f \); full-wave ripple frequency \( =2f \)
topics.worked_example:
A 10 V Zener with a 250 \( \Omega \) series resistor runs from 15 V and feeds a 1 k\( \Omega \) load. Find the Zener current.

\( I_R=(15-10)/250=20 \) mA and \( I_L=10/1000=10 \) mA, so \( I_Z=20-10=10 \) mA.
common_mistakes: Giving a full-wave rectifier the same ripple frequency as a half-wave rectifier
Thinking a Zener regulates in forward bias
Assuming an ordinary diode regulates just as well in reverse breakdown
Swapping the LED (forward bias) and photodiode (reverse bias) conventions
Thinking a solar cell needs an external battery

topics.name: Bipolar Junction Transistor: Structure, Transistor Action, and Current Relations
topics.summary: A bipolar junction transistor has three regions, emitter, base and collector, arranged as n-p-n or p-n-p, with two junctions. The emitter is heavily doped to supply many majority carriers; the base is very thin and lightly doped so that few carriers recombine there; the collector is the largest region and is moderately doped. In the active region the emitter-base junction is forward biased and the collector-base junction reverse biased. Carriers injected by the emitter cross the base, and most are swept into the collector. By charge conservation \( I_E=I_B+I_C \), with \( I_B \) always the smallest current. The common-base current gain \( \alpha=I_C/I_E \) is always slightly less than 1, typically 0.95 to 0.99. The common-emitter current gain \( \beta=I_C/I_B \) is always greater than 1, usually tens to hundreds. They are linked by \( \beta=\dfrac{\alpha}{1-\alpha} \) and \( \alpha=\dfrac{\beta}{1+\beta} \). The CE input characteristic plots \( I_B \) against \( V_{BE} \); the output characteristic plots \( I_C \) against \( V_{CE} \).
topics.worked_example:
A transistor has \( \alpha=0.98 \) and \( I_E=10 \) mA. Find \( I_C \), \( I_B \) and \( \beta \).

\( I_C=0.98\times10=9.8 \) mA, \( I_B=10-9.8=0.2 \) mA, and \( \beta=9.8/0.2=49 \), which matches \( 0.98/0.02=49 \).
common_mistakes: Writing \( I_E=I_C \) and leaving out \( I_B \)
Reporting \( \alpha \) greater than 1 or \( \beta \) less than 1
Swapping \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) between the common-base and common-emitter configurations
Thinking the base is thick or heavily doped
Mixing up the input and output characteristics

topics.name: Transistor as an Amplifier and Switch, and Digital Electronics: Logic Gates
topics.summary: For amplification a transistor must be in the active region: emitter-base forward biased and collector-base reverse biased. In a common-emitter amplifier, a small change in \( I_B \) produces a change \( \beta \) times larger in \( I_C \), and the voltage gain is \( A_v=-\beta\left(\dfrac{R_C}{R_{in}}\right) \). The minus sign means the output is \( 180^\circ \) out of phase with the input, because a larger \( I_C \) increases the drop across \( R_C \) and lowers \( V_{CE} \). As a switch, the transistor uses cutoff (both junctions reverse biased, output high) and saturation (both forward biased, output low), so it acts as a NOT gate. Logic gates: AND, \( Y=A\cdot B \), gives 1 only when all inputs are 1; OR, \( Y=A+B \), gives 1 when any input is 1; NOT gives \( Y=\overline{A} \); NAND is \( \overline{A\cdot B} \) and NOR is \( \overline{A+B} \). NAND and NOR are the universal gates, since each alone can build every other basic gate.
topics.worked_example:
A CE amplifier has \( \beta=50 \), \( R_C=4 \) k\( \Omega \), \( R_{in}=2 \) k\( \Omega \) and a 20 mV input. Find the output.

\( |A_v|=50\times4/2=100 \), so the output is \( 100\times20 \) mV \( =2 \) V, inverted relative to the input.
common_mistakes: Biasing either junction the wrong way for amplification
Thinking the CE output is in phase with the input
Swapping the AND and OR truth-table conditions
Calling AND and OR the universal gates instead of NAND and NOR
Using the active region for switching instead of cutoff and saturation

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Classification of Solids and Intrinsic/Extrinsic Semiconductors: p-type and n-type
questions.question: Silicon is doped with a small amount of phosphorus (a pentavalent element). What type of semiconductor is formed?
options: n-type, because each phosphorus atom donates a free electron
p-type, because each phosphorus atom creates a hole
Intrinsic, because phosphorus does not change the carrier balance
p-type, because phosphorus accepts an electron from silicon
questions.explanation:
Phosphorus has 5 valence electrons. Four of them form covalent bonds with neighbouring silicon atoms.

The fifth electron is loosely bound and easily becomes free, so phosphorus acts as a donor.

Extra free electrons make the material n-type.
questions.hint: Count the valence electrons: 5 is one more than silicon needs for its four bonds.
distractor_logic: Swaps pentavalent with p-type: a hole is created by a trivalent impurity, not a pentavalent one
Ignores that the fifth valence electron of phosphorus is left free, so electrons now outnumber holes
Treats phosphorus as an acceptor; it is a donor since it has one electron more than silicon needs for bonding

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Classification of Solids and Intrinsic/Extrinsic Semiconductors: p-type and n-type
questions.question: In a p-type semiconductor, which charge carriers are in the majority?
options: Electrons and holes in exactly equal numbers
questions.explanation:
A p-type semiconductor is made by adding a trivalent impurity such as boron.

Each trivalent atom leaves one bond incomplete, creating a hole.

So holes greatly outnumber electrons: holes are the majority carriers and electrons are the minority carriers.
questions.hint: The letter p stands for positive, the sign of the charge a hole behaves as having.
distractor_logic: Swaps majority and minority: electrons are the majority carriers only in n-type material
Equal numbers of electrons and holes describe an intrinsic (undoped) semiconductor
Ions in the lattice are fixed in place and cannot carry current; also p-type material contains acceptor ions, not donor ions

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Classification of Solids and Intrinsic/Extrinsic Semiconductors: p-type and n-type
questions.question: The energy band gap of silicon at room temperature is approximately:
questions.explanation:
Semiconductors have a small band gap between the valence and conduction bands.

For silicon this gap is about 1.1 eV, and for germanium it is about 0.7 eV.

Insulators have gaps larger than 3 eV, while in conductors the bands overlap.
questions.hint: Silicon's gap is slightly larger than germanium's but far smaller than an insulator's.
distractor_logic: About 0.7 eV is the band gap of germanium, not silicon
A gap larger than 3 eV is typical of an insulator, not a semiconductor
Overlapping bands with no gap describe a conductor (metal)

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Classification of Solids and Intrinsic/Extrinsic Semiconductors: p-type and n-type
questions.question: As the temperature of a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor increases, its electrical conductivity:
options: decreases, because the lattice vibrates more, just as in a metal
stays constant, because the band gap does not depend on temperature
falls to zero, because the holes and electrons recombine faster
increases, because more electrons are thermally excited across the band gap
questions.explanation:
At higher temperature, more electrons gain enough thermal energy to jump from the valence band to the conduction band.

Each jump creates a free electron and a hole, so the number of charge carriers rises.

Therefore conductivity increases with temperature, which is the opposite of the trend in metals.
questions.hint: Think about what heat does to the number of carriers, not just to their motion.
distractor_logic: Applies the metal trend to a semiconductor; in a semiconductor the rise in carrier number far outweighs extra scattering
Ignores that the number of carriers crossing the gap depends strongly on temperature
Reverses the effect: heating generates electron-hole pairs faster, so the carrier count grows

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Classification of Solids and Intrinsic/Extrinsic Semiconductors: p-type and n-type
questions.question: In an intrinsic semiconductor, the number density of free electrons \( n_e \) and holes \( n_h \) are related as:
questions.explanation:
In a pure semiconductor, every electron that jumps to the conduction band leaves exactly one hole behind in the valence band.

So electrons and holes are created in pairs, giving \( n_e=n_h=n_i \), where \( n_i \) is the intrinsic carrier concentration.
questions.hint: Each thermally freed electron leaves exactly one vacancy behind.
distractor_logic: Electrons exceed holes only in an n-type (doped) semiconductor
Holes exceed electrons only in a p-type (doped) semiconductor
At room temperature some electrons are always thermally excited, so \( n_e \) is not zero

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Classification of Solids and Intrinsic/Extrinsic Semiconductors: p-type and n-type
questions.question: In the energy band diagram of a good conductor such as copper:
options: the bands are separated by a small gap of about 1 eV
the valence band and conduction band overlap
the bands are separated by a large gap of more than 3 eV
the conduction band is completely filled and the valence band is empty
questions.explanation:
In metals, the conduction band either overlaps the valence band or is partly filled.

Electrons can therefore move into empty energy states with almost no extra energy, which makes the material a good conductor.
questions.hint: A conductor needs no energy input for electrons to start moving.
distractor_logic: A small gap of about 1 eV describes a semiconductor
A large gap greater than 3 eV describes an insulator
Inverts the normal filling order; electrons fill the lower (valence) band first

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Classification of Solids and Intrinsic/Extrinsic Semiconductors: p-type and n-type
questions.question: A trivalent impurity such as boron added to silicon is called:
questions.explanation:
Boron has only 3 valence electrons, so one of the four bonds with neighbouring silicon atoms is left incomplete.

This vacancy (hole) can accept an electron from a nearby bond, so boron is called an acceptor impurity and produces p-type material.
questions.hint: Ask whether the impurity gives away an electron or takes one in.
distractor_logic: Donors are pentavalent atoms that give away an extra electron; boron does the opposite
An intrinsic semiconductor has no impurity at all, so the phrase does not classify a dopant
Boron has 3 valence electrons, so it is trivalent, not pentavalent

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Classification of Solids and Intrinsic/Extrinsic Semiconductors: p-type and n-type
questions.question: An n-type semiconductor has many more free electrons than holes. Overall, the n-type crystal is:
options: neutral only at 0 K and negatively charged above it
questions.explanation:
Each donor atom is neutral before it gives up its extra electron.

After ionisation, the free electron and the fixed positive donor ion together still carry zero net charge.

So the whole crystal stays electrically neutral even though electrons are the majority carriers.
questions.hint: Doping adds neutral atoms; nothing adds net charge.
distractor_logic: Forgets that every free electron came from a donor atom that is left as a positive ion, so the charges balance
Donor ions are positive, but the free electrons they release cancel that charge exactly
Heating creates electron-hole pairs, and each pair is neutral, so neutrality holds at every temperature

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: p-n Junction Diode: Depletion Region, Barrier Potential, and Forward/Reverse Bias
questions.question: When a p-n junction is forward biased, the width of its depletion region:
options: becomes zero permanently even after the bias is removed
questions.explanation:
In forward bias, the applied voltage opposes the built-in barrier potential.

Majority carriers are pushed towards the junction, neutralising some of the fixed ions, so the depletion region becomes narrower and current flows easily.
questions.hint: Forward bias makes it easier for current to flow; picture the barrier shrinking.
distractor_logic: Increase in depletion width happens under reverse bias, not forward bias
Ignores that the applied voltage opposes the barrier and pushes majority carriers into the depletion region
The depletion region re-forms as soon as the external voltage is removed

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: p-n Junction Diode: Depletion Region, Barrier Potential, and Forward/Reverse Bias
questions.question: For a p-n junction diode to be forward biased, the terminals of the battery must be connected as:
options: p-side to the negative terminal and n-side to the positive terminal
p-side to the positive terminal and n-side to the negative terminal
both p-side and n-side to the positive terminal
n-side to the positive terminal with the p-side left unconnected
questions.explanation:
Forward bias means the external voltage opposes the barrier potential.

The p-side must be at the higher potential, so it connects to the positive terminal while the n-side connects to the negative terminal.
questions.hint: Match p with positive.
distractor_logic: This is the reverse-bias connection, which widens the depletion region
No potential difference is applied across the junction this way, so it is not biased at all
An open p-side means no complete circuit, so no bias of either kind is applied

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: p-n Junction Diode: Depletion Region, Barrier Potential, and Forward/Reverse Bias
questions.question: The barrier potential of a silicon p-n junction is approximately:
questions.explanation:
The built-in barrier potential for a silicon p-n junction is about 0.7 V.

For germanium it is about 0.3 V. A forward voltage larger than this is needed before the diode conducts appreciably.
questions.hint: Silicon's barrier is a little under one volt.
distractor_logic: About 0.3 V is the barrier potential of a germanium junction
Confuses the silicon band gap of about 1.1 eV with the junction barrier potential
Off by a factor of ten; several volts would be typical of a breakdown voltage, not a barrier potential

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: p-n Junction Diode: Depletion Region, Barrier Potential, and Forward/Reverse Bias
questions.question: The depletion region of an unbiased p-n junction contains:
options: mobile ions that carry the current across the junction
immobile ions and practically no free charge carriers
questions.explanation:
Near the junction, electrons from the n-side and holes from the p-side diffuse across and recombine.

This leaves behind fixed positive donor ions on the n-side and fixed negative acceptor ions on the p-side.

The region is depleted of mobile carriers, hence the name depletion region.
questions.hint: The name of the region tells you what it lacks.
distractor_logic: Free electrons that reach this region recombine with holes, so it is depleted of free electrons too
Holes that diffuse in recombine with electrons, so the region is also depleted of holes
Ions are locked in the crystal lattice and cannot move to carry current

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: p-n Junction Diode: Depletion Region, Barrier Potential, and Forward/Reverse Bias
questions.question: The small current that flows through a reverse-biased p-n junction (below breakdown) is mainly due to:
options: drift of minority carriers across the junction
diffusion of majority carriers across the junction
movement of the donor and acceptor ions
electrons tunnelling from the battery terminals
questions.explanation:
Reverse bias increases the barrier, so majority carriers cannot cross.

However, the field in the depletion region sweeps minority carriers (electrons on the p-side, holes on the n-side) across the junction.

This drift of minority carriers produces the tiny reverse current.
questions.hint: Which carriers find the reverse-bias field helping them across?
distractor_logic: Majority-carrier diffusion dominates in forward bias; reverse bias raises the barrier and blocks it
The ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move
No tunnelling from the terminals is involved; the reverse current comes from thermally generated minority carriers

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: p-n Junction Diode: Depletion Region, Barrier Potential, and Forward/Reverse Bias
questions.question: The reverse saturation current of a p-n junction diode depends strongly on:
options: the magnitude of the applied reverse voltage
the length of the connecting wires
the colour of the diode's casing
questions.explanation:
The reverse current is carried by minority carriers, which are produced by thermal generation of electron-hole pairs.

Their number is limited by temperature, not by the applied voltage, so the current saturates with voltage but rises sharply as temperature rises.
questions.hint: What produces minority carriers in the first place?
distractor_logic: Below breakdown the reverse current is almost independent of reverse voltage; this is the central trap
Connecting wires do not affect the rate at which minority carriers are generated
Casing colour has no effect on the carrier generation inside the junction

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: p-n Junction Diode: Depletion Region, Barrier Potential, and Forward/Reverse Bias
questions.question: The depletion region in a p-n junction is formed initially because of:
options: drift of carriers due to an external battery
removal of all impurity atoms near the junction
diffusion of majority carriers across the junction and their recombination
heating of the junction during manufacture
questions.explanation:
Holes are concentrated on the p-side and electrons on the n-side.

This concentration difference makes them diffuse across the junction, where they recombine.

The fixed ions left behind form the depletion region and set up the barrier potential.
questions.hint: Carriers move from where there are many to where there are few.
distractor_logic: No battery is needed; the depletion region exists even in an unbiased junction
The impurity atoms stay in place; it is the carriers that are removed, leaving ionised impurities behind
Temperature during manufacture is not the cause; the concentration difference of carriers drives diffusion

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: p-n Junction Diode: Depletion Region, Barrier Potential, and Forward/Reverse Bias
questions.question: The resistance offered by a p-n junction diode in reverse bias (below breakdown) is:
options: the same as in forward bias
questions.explanation:
In reverse bias only a tiny minority-carrier current flows even for a large reverse voltage.

Since \( R=V/I \) with a large \( V \) and very small \( I \), the reverse resistance is very high.
questions.hint: Large voltage with almost no current means what kind of resistance?
distractor_logic: Very low resistance is the forward-bias behaviour
Ignores the one-way nature of the diode; forward and reverse resistances differ enormously
Zero resistance would mean unlimited current, the opposite of reverse-bias behaviour

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Diode Applications: Rectifiers, and Zener, LED, Photodiode, and Solar Cell Devices
questions.question: A half-wave rectifier is fed with a 50 Hz AC input. The ripple frequency of its output is:
options: 0 Hz, since the output is pure DC
questions.explanation:
A half-wave rectifier passes only one half-cycle in each complete input cycle.

So there is one output pulse per input cycle, and the ripple frequency equals the input frequency, 50 Hz.
questions.hint: Count output pulses per input cycle.
distractor_logic: Double the input frequency is the full-wave result, not the half-wave one
Halving the frequency has no basis; one output pulse appears in every input cycle
The rectified output is pulsating, not smooth DC, so it has a ripple frequency

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Diode Applications: Rectifiers, and Zener, LED, Photodiode, and Solar Cell Devices
questions.question: To work as a voltage regulator, a Zener diode is operated in:
options: reverse bias below the breakdown voltage
questions.explanation:
In reverse breakdown, the voltage across a Zener diode stays nearly constant at \( V_Z \) over a wide range of current.

This property is used to keep the output voltage steady, so the Zener is deliberately operated in reverse breakdown.
questions.hint: The Zener's useful constant voltage appears only after breakdown.
distractor_logic: Forward bias gives only the small barrier drop and is not how a Zener regulates
An unbiased diode carries no current and cannot hold a voltage constant
Below breakdown the reverse current is tiny and the voltage is not held fixed

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Diode Applications: Rectifiers, and Zener, LED, Photodiode, and Solar Cell Devices
questions.question: A light-emitting diode (LED) emits light when it is:
questions.explanation:
In forward bias, electrons and holes are injected across the junction and recombine.

In an LED, the energy released in each recombination is emitted as a photon, so light is produced only under forward bias.
questions.hint: Light comes from recombination, which needs current to flow.
distractor_logic: Reverse bias gives almost no current, so there is no recombination to emit light; this is photodiode biasing
Reverse breakdown is the Zener's operating mode, not the LED's
Light falling on an unbiased junction is the solar-cell action; an LED needs current to emit light

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Diode Applications: Rectifiers, and Zener, LED, Photodiode, and Solar Cell Devices
questions.question: A photodiode is normally operated in:
options: the unbiased condition, like a solar cell
questions.explanation:
Under reverse bias, the dark current is very small.

Light creates electron-hole pairs near the junction, and the reverse current increases noticeably with light intensity, which makes detection easy.
questions.hint: A detector works best when the signal changes a small current by a large fraction.
distractor_logic: Forward bias is the LED convention; the photo-generated change would be tiny compared with the large forward current
Breakdown is the Zener's operating mode and would swamp the light-dependent current
The unbiased mode belongs to the solar cell, which generates an EMF rather than detecting light

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Diode Applications: Rectifiers, and Zener, LED, Photodiode, and Solar Cell Devices
questions.question: A solar cell produces electrical energy because:
options: incident light generates electron-hole pairs at an unbiased p-n junction, producing an EMF
it is forward biased by a battery and emits light
it is reverse biased by a battery and its breakdown voltage drives current
heat from sunlight makes the metal contacts emit electrons
questions.explanation:
In a solar cell no external bias is applied.

Photons with energy greater than the band gap create electron-hole pairs near the junction, and the built-in field separates them.

This separation produces an EMF that can drive current through an external load.
questions.hint: A solar cell is a source of EMF, so it needs no battery.
distractor_logic: Describes an LED; a solar cell needs no battery and absorbs rather than emits light
Describes Zener breakdown; a solar cell is a source, not a biased load
The effect is due to photons creating carriers in the semiconductor, not heating of the contacts

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Diode Applications: Rectifiers, and Zener, LED, Photodiode, and Solar Cell Devices
questions.question: The main function of a rectifier is to:
options: convert direct current into alternating current
convert alternating current into (pulsating) direct current
increase the amplitude of an AC signal
questions.explanation:
A diode conducts only when forward biased.

A rectifier uses this one-way conduction to let current through in only one direction, turning AC into unidirectional (pulsating) DC.
questions.hint: Use the diode's one-way conduction.
distractor_logic: Converting DC into AC is the job of an inverter or oscillator, not a rectifier
Increasing amplitude is amplification, performed by a transistor circuit
Storing charge is done by a capacitor

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Diode Applications: Rectifiers, and Zener, LED, Photodiode, and Solar Cell Devices
questions.question: A full-wave rectifier is more efficient than a half-wave rectifier because it:
options: uses both half-cycles of the AC input
questions.explanation:
In a full-wave rectifier, one set of diodes conducts in the positive half-cycle and another set in the negative half-cycle.

Current flows through the load in the same direction during both halves, so no half-cycle is wasted.
questions.hint: The word full refers to how much of each cycle is used.
distractor_logic: Using only one half-cycle is exactly what a half-wave rectifier does
Using just one half-cycle, whichever it is, still wastes the other half
All rectifiers need diodes; a full-wave circuit uses two (centre-tap) or four (bridge)

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Diode Applications: Rectifiers, and Zener, LED, Photodiode, and Solar Cell Devices
questions.question: The most common use of a Zener diode is as a:
questions.explanation:
A Zener diode in reverse breakdown keeps the voltage across it nearly constant even when the current through it changes.

Placed in parallel with a load, it holds the load voltage steady, so it serves as a voltage regulator.
questions.hint: Think about what stays constant in the Zener's breakdown region.
distractor_logic: Rectification uses ordinary diodes in forward conduction, not Zener breakdown
Current amplification requires a transistor, which has three terminals
Emitting light is the job of an LED under forward bias

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Bipolar Junction Transistor: Structure, Transistor Action, and Current Relations
questions.question: The emitter, base and collector currents of a transistor are related by:
questions.explanation:
Charge carriers entering from the emitter divide: a small fraction leaves through the base, and the rest reaches the collector.

By charge conservation, \( I_E=I_B+I_C \).
questions.hint: The emitter current splits into two parts.
distractor_logic: Omits the base current, which is small but never zero
Makes the collector current the largest, but the emitter current is the one that splits into the other two
Makes the base current the largest, though it is actually the smallest of the three

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Bipolar Junction Transistor: Structure, Transistor Action, and Current Relations
questions.question: Among the three transistor currents \( I_E,I_B,I_C \), the smallest is:
options: none, since all three are equal
questions.explanation:
The base is thin and lightly doped, so only a few injected carriers recombine there.

Most carriers pass on to the collector, so \( I_B \) is only a small fraction of \( I_E \) and is the smallest of the three currents.
questions.hint: Which region is thin and lightly doped?
distractor_logic: The emitter current is the largest, being the sum of the other two
The collector current is nearly as large as the emitter current
The currents cannot be equal, since \( I_E=I_B+I_C \)

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Bipolar Junction Transistor: Structure, Transistor Action, and Current Relations
questions.question: In a bipolar junction transistor, the most heavily doped region is the:
options: none, since all three regions are equally doped
questions.explanation:
The emitter must supply a large number of majority carriers into the base.

So it is heavily doped, while the base is lightly doped and the collector is moderately doped.
questions.hint: Which region supplies the charge carriers?
distractor_logic: The base is the most lightly doped region, not the most heavily doped
The collector is moderately doped; its distinctive feature is its large size
Equal doping would stop the transistor from working, since each region has a different job

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Bipolar Junction Transistor: Structure, Transistor Action, and Current Relations
questions.question: The base of a transistor is made:
questions.explanation:
Carriers injected from the emitter must cross the base to reach the collector.

A thin, lightly doped base lets most of them pass without recombining, which keeps \( I_B \) small and \( I_C \) large.
questions.hint: The base should let carriers pass without trapping them.
distractor_logic: A thick, heavily doped base would recombine most carriers, making \( I_B \) large and the gain small
Heavy doping of the base would cause many recombinations even if it were thin
A thick base gives carriers more time to recombine, so few would reach the collector

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Bipolar Junction Transistor: Structure, Transistor Action, and Current Relations
questions.question: The common-emitter current gain \( \beta \) is defined as:
questions.explanation:
In the common-emitter configuration, the input current is \( I_B \) and the output current is \( I_C \).

So the current gain is \( \beta=I_C/I_B \), which is usually large (tens to hundreds).
questions.hint: Output current divided by input current, in common-emitter mode.
distractor_logic: \( I_C/I_E \) is the common-base gain \( \alpha \), not \( \beta \)
Inverts the ratio, which would give a number much less than 1
Uses the emitter current as the output, but in common-emitter mode the output current is \( I_C \)

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Bipolar Junction Transistor: Structure, Transistor Action, and Current Relations
questions.question: The value of the common-base current gain \( \alpha \) of a transistor is:
options: typically in the range of tens to hundreds
questions.explanation:
\( \alpha=I_C/I_E \), and since \( I_E=I_B+I_C \), the collector current is always a little smaller than the emitter current.

So \( \alpha \) is slightly less than 1, typically about 0.95 to 0.99.
questions.hint: Compare \( I_C \) with \( I_E \).
distractor_logic: \( \alpha=I_C/I_E \) cannot exceed 1 because \( I_C \) is always less than \( I_E \)
Exactly 1 would need \( I_B=0 \), but some base current always flows
Tens to hundreds is the typical range of \( \beta \), not \( \alpha \)

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Bipolar Junction Transistor: Structure, Transistor Action, and Current Relations
questions.question: How many p-n junctions does a bipolar junction transistor have?
questions.explanation:
A transistor has three regions (emitter, base, collector) arranged as n-p-n or p-n-p.

The two boundaries give two junctions: the emitter-base junction and the collector-base junction.
questions.hint: Three layers, count the boundaries.
distractor_logic: One junction makes a diode, not a transistor
Three regions form only two boundaries between neighbouring layers
Double counts; a three-layer structure has only two junctions

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Bipolar Junction Transistor: Structure, Transistor Action, and Current Relations
questions.question: In a transistor, the region that is largest in size is the:
options: emitter and base, which are equal
questions.explanation:
The collector must collect most of the carriers and dissipate more heat, since it carries a large current at a larger voltage.

So it is made the largest region, with moderate doping.
questions.hint: Which region must handle the most power?
distractor_logic: The emitter's distinctive feature is heavy doping, not large size
The base is the thinnest region
The emitter and base are neither equal nor the largest

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Transistor as an Amplifier and Switch, and Digital Electronics: Logic Gates
questions.question: A two-input AND gate gives output 1 when:
questions.explanation:
The AND gate is described by \( Y=A\cdot B \).

The product is 1 only when \( A=1 \) and \( B=1 \); every other combination gives 0.
questions.hint: AND means this one and that one.
distractor_logic: Output 1 for any input being 1 is the OR gate condition
Output 1 for both inputs 0 is the NOR gate condition
Output 1 for at least one input being 0 is the NAND gate condition

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Transistor as an Amplifier and Switch, and Digital Electronics: Logic Gates
questions.question: The gates called universal gates, from which every other basic gate can be built, are:
questions.explanation:
Using only NAND gates, one can build NOT, AND and OR gates; the same is true using only NOR gates.

That is why NAND and NOR are called universal gates.
questions.hint: A universal gate must be able to invert on its own.
distractor_logic: AND and OR alone cannot produce inversion, so they cannot build a NOT gate
A combination of two gates is not what universal means; each universal gate works on its own
Pairing two basic gates does not make either one universal

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Transistor as an Amplifier and Switch, and Digital Electronics: Logic Gates
questions.question: The Boolean expression for a NOT gate with input \( A \) is:
questions.explanation:
A NOT gate inverts its single input: when \( A=0 \), \( Y=1 \), and when \( A=1 \), \( Y=0 \).

This is written \( Y=\overline{A} \).
questions.hint: The output must always be the opposite of the input.
distractor_logic: Output equal to input is a buffer, with no inversion
\( A\cdot A=A \), so this also gives no inversion
\( A+A=A \), so this too leaves the input unchanged

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Transistor as an Amplifier and Switch, and Digital Electronics: Logic Gates
questions.question: For a transistor to work as an amplifier, its junctions must be biased as:
options: emitter-base reverse biased and collector-base forward biased
emitter-base forward biased and collector-base reverse biased
questions.explanation:
Amplification needs the active region.

A forward-biased emitter-base junction injects carriers into the base, and a reverse-biased collector-base junction sweeps them into the collector, so a small change in \( I_B \) controls a large change in \( I_C \).
questions.hint: Emitter injects, collector collects.
distractor_logic: Swaps the two junctions; this does not put the transistor in the active region
Both junctions forward biased gives saturation, used for the ON state of a switch
Both junctions reverse biased gives cutoff, used for the OFF state of a switch

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Transistor as an Amplifier and Switch, and Digital Electronics: Logic Gates
questions.question: In a common-emitter amplifier, the phase difference between the output voltage and the input voltage is:
options: \( 0^\circ \), since the output is in phase with the input
questions.explanation:
When the input increases, \( I_B \) and hence \( I_C \) increase, so the voltage drop across \( R_C \) grows.

The collector voltage therefore falls, so the output is inverted: a phase difference of \( 180^\circ \).
questions.hint: Does the collector voltage rise or fall when the base current rises?
distractor_logic: The common-emitter output is inverted, not in phase; this is the central trap
A quarter-cycle shift is typical of a pure capacitor or inductor, not a CE amplifier
No step in the amplifier's action produces a one-eighth-cycle shift

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Transistor as an Amplifier and Switch, and Digital Electronics: Logic Gates
questions.question: The Boolean expression for a two-input OR gate is:
questions.explanation:
An OR gate gives 1 when either input (or both) is 1.

This is written as a Boolean sum, \( Y=A+B \).
questions.hint: In Boolean algebra, OR is written as addition.
distractor_logic: \( Y=A\cdot B \) is the AND gate
\( Y=\overline{A+B} \) is the NOR gate, the inverted OR
\( Y=\overline{A\cdot B} \) is the NAND gate

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Transistor as an Amplifier and Switch, and Digital Electronics: Logic Gates
questions.question: When a transistor is used as a switch, it is operated in:
options: the active and cutoff regions only
questions.explanation:
A switch needs two clear states.

In cutoff almost no collector current flows (switch OFF), and in saturation a large collector current flows with nearly zero \( V_{CE} \) (switch ON).
questions.hint: A switch is either fully OFF or fully ON.
distractor_logic: The active region is used for amplification, where the output varies smoothly
The active region is not a switch state; the ON state is saturation
Breakdown can damage the transistor and is not a switching state

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Transistor as an Amplifier and Switch, and Digital Electronics: Logic Gates
questions.question: A two-input NOR gate gives output 1 when:
questions.explanation:
NOR is \( Y=\overline{A+B} \).

\( A+B \) is 0 only when both inputs are 0, so the NOR output is 1 only for \( A=0 \) and \( B=0 \).
questions.hint: First find when OR gives 0, then invert.
distractor_logic: Both inputs 1 makes \( A+B=1 \), so NOR gives 0
With exactly one input at 1, \( A+B=1 \), so NOR gives 0
Output 1 when any input is 1 is the OR condition, which NOR inverts

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Classification of Solids and Intrinsic/Extrinsic Semiconductors: p-type and n-type
questions.question: Pure silicon has an intrinsic carrier concentration \( n_i=1.5\times10^{16}\,\text{m}^{-3} \). It is doped with a pentavalent impurity so that the electron concentration becomes \( n_e=10^{22}\,\text{m}^{-3} \). Using \( n_e n_h=n_i^2 \), the hole concentration is:
questions.explanation:
By the mass-action law, \( n_h=n_i^2/n_e \).

\( n_i^2=(1.5\times10^{16})^2=2.25\times10^{32} \).

\( n_h=2.25\times10^{32}/10^{22}=2.25\times10^{10}\,\text{m}^{-3} \), far smaller than \( n_e \), as expected for minority carriers.
questions.hint: Square \( n_i \), then divide by the majority-carrier concentration.
distractor_logic: Assumes the hole concentration stays at the intrinsic value, ignoring that extra electrons increase recombination
Gives holes the majority-carrier value; in n-type material holes are the minority
Computes \( n_i^2 \) but forgets to divide by \( n_e \)

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Classification of Solids and Intrinsic/Extrinsic Semiconductors: p-type and n-type
questions.question: Silicon is doped with arsenic. Which statement correctly describes the resulting material?
options: p-type, with holes as majority carriers and electrons as minority carriers
n-type, with electrons as majority carriers and holes as minority carriers
n-type, with holes as majority carriers and electrons as minority carriers
p-type, with electrons as majority carriers and holes as minority carriers
questions.explanation:
Arsenic is pentavalent, so each atom donates one free electron.

The material is therefore n-type: electrons are the majority carriers and holes are the minority carriers.
questions.hint: Arsenic sits in the same group as phosphorus.
distractor_logic: Swaps pentavalent with p-type; arsenic has 5 valence electrons and is a donor
Gets the type right but swaps the majority and minority carriers
Wrong type and a carrier pairing that contradicts the meaning of p-type

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Classification of Solids and Intrinsic/Extrinsic Semiconductors: p-type and n-type
questions.question: Germanium is doped with indium (a trivalent element). The minority charge carriers in this material are:
options: electrons and holes equally, since germanium is intrinsic
questions.explanation:
Indium has 3 valence electrons, so it creates holes and gives p-type germanium.

In p-type material, holes are the majority carriers and electrons are the minority carriers.
questions.hint: First decide the type, then name the less numerous carrier.
distractor_logic: Holes are the majority carriers in indium-doped (p-type) germanium
Indium ions are fixed in the lattice and do not carry current at all
Once doped, germanium is extrinsic, so electron and hole numbers are no longer equal

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Classification of Solids and Intrinsic/Extrinsic Semiconductors: p-type and n-type
questions.question: Silicon has a band gap of 1.1 eV while diamond has a band gap of 5.4 eV. At room temperature, why does silicon conduct far better than diamond?
options: Silicon's valence and conduction bands overlap, while diamond's do not
Diamond's larger gap means more electrons jump across it at room temperature
Both have the same number of free electrons; silicon's are simply faster
Its small gap lets many electrons be thermally excited into the conduction band, while diamond's gap is too large for this
questions.explanation:
Thermal energy at room temperature can lift a significant number of electrons across a gap of about 1.1 eV.

A gap of 5.4 eV is typical of an insulator (greater than 3 eV), so almost no electrons cross it.

So silicon has many more free carriers and conducts much better.
questions.hint: Compare each gap with the insulator threshold of about 3 eV.
distractor_logic: Silicon has a real gap of about 1.1 eV; overlapping bands describe a metal
Reverses the effect: a larger gap means fewer electrons can be thermally excited
The difference lies in how many carriers are available, not in their speed

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Classification of Solids and Intrinsic/Extrinsic Semiconductors: p-type and n-type
questions.question: A crystalline solid has an energy band gap of 0.7 eV. At room temperature it would be classified as a:
questions.explanation:
A small but non-zero gap (roughly 0.5 eV to 3 eV) marks a semiconductor.

0.7 eV is in fact the band gap of germanium, a standard semiconductor.
questions.hint: Place 0.7 eV between zero and 3 eV.
distractor_logic: A conductor has overlapping bands with no gap
An insulator has a gap larger than about 3 eV
Superconductivity is unrelated to having a small band gap and is outside this chapter

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Classification of Solids and Intrinsic/Extrinsic Semiconductors: p-type and n-type
questions.question: Silicon contains about \( 5\times10^{28} \) atoms per cubic metre. If it is doped with one arsenic atom for every \( 10^{6} \) silicon atoms, the number density of donor atoms is:
questions.explanation:
One donor per \( 10^{6} \) atoms means dividing the atom density by \( 10^{6} \).

\( N_D=5\times10^{28}/10^{6}=5\times10^{22}\,\text{m}^{-3} \).
questions.hint: A 1-in-a-million doping ratio means divide by a million.
distractor_logic: Multiplies by \( 10^{6} \) instead of dividing
Ignores the doping ratio and takes every silicon atom as a donor
Takes the ratio itself as the number density

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Classification of Solids and Intrinsic/Extrinsic Semiconductors: p-type and n-type
questions.question: An electric field is applied across an intrinsic semiconductor. How do the electron and hole contributions to the current compare in direction?
options: Electrons and holes move in opposite directions, so their currents cancel
Only electrons contribute; holes cannot move
Electrons and holes move in opposite directions, but both contribute current in the same direction
Electrons and holes move in the same direction, so their currents cancel
questions.explanation:
Electrons drift opposite to the field, and holes (behaving as positive charges) drift along the field.

A negative charge moving one way and a positive charge moving the other way both give conventional current along the field.

So the total current is \( I=I_e+I_h \).
questions.hint: Moving negative charge left is the same current as moving positive charge right.
distractor_logic: Opposite charges moving in opposite directions give current in the same direction, so nothing cancels
Holes do move effectively, as neighbouring bound electrons fill them one after another
Opposite charges experience forces in opposite directions, so they cannot drift the same way

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Classification of Solids and Intrinsic/Extrinsic Semiconductors: p-type and n-type
questions.question: Adding a very small amount of pentavalent impurity (about 1 atom per million) increases the conductivity of silicon enormously. The main reason is that:
options: the impurity reduces silicon's band gap from 1.1 eV to zero
the impurity atoms themselves move through the crystal carrying charge
the impurity increases the number of holes in the valence band
the donor energy level lies just below the conduction band, so donor electrons are freed very easily
questions.explanation:
The fifth electron of a donor needs only about 0.01 eV to 0.05 eV to become free, far less than the 1.1 eV gap.

So at room temperature almost every donor is ionised, adding a huge number of free electrons compared with the few thermally generated ones.
questions.hint: Compare the energy needed to free a donor electron with the band gap.
distractor_logic: Doping this light does not remove the band gap; silicon remains a semiconductor
Impurity atoms are fixed in the lattice; only their released electrons move
A pentavalent donor increases electrons, not holes; holes are increased by trivalent doping

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: p-n Junction Diode: Depletion Region, Barrier Potential, and Forward/Reverse Bias
questions.question: A forward-biased diode carries a current of 20 mA when the voltage across it is 0.8 V. Its static forward resistance at this point is:
questions.hint: Convert the current to amperes before dividing.
distractor_logic: Multiplies \( V \) and \( I \) instead of dividing
Divides 0.8 by 20 without converting mA to A
Takes the reciprocal ratio \( I/V \) in mixed units

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: p-n Junction Diode: Depletion Region, Barrier Potential, and Forward/Reverse Bias
questions.question: A silicon diode (barrier potential 0.7 V) is connected in forward bias in series with a 1 k\( \Omega \) resistor across a 5.7 V battery. The current in the circuit is:
questions.explanation:
The voltage across the resistor is \( 5.7-0.7=5.0 \) V.

\( I=5.0/1000=5\times10^{-3} \) A, which is 5 mA.
questions.hint: Subtract the diode drop before applying Ohm's law.
distractor_logic: Ignores the 0.7 V drop across the forward-biased diode
Adds the barrier potential to the supply instead of subtracting it
Treats the forward-biased diode as blocking; it conducts once the barrier is exceeded

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: p-n Junction Diode: Depletion Region, Barrier Potential, and Forward/Reverse Bias
questions.question: In the circuit of a 5.7 V battery, a 1 k\( \Omega \) resistor and a silicon diode, the diode is now reversed so that it is reverse biased (well below breakdown). The current is approximately:
options: 5 mA, the same as in forward bias
5.7 mA, since the barrier drop no longer applies
practically zero (a tiny reverse current only)
very large, since reverse bias lowers the barrier
questions.explanation:
In reverse bias the depletion region widens and the barrier rises, so majority carriers cannot cross.

Only a tiny minority-carrier current flows, so the circuit current is practically zero.
questions.hint: A diode is a one-way valve.
distractor_logic: Ignores that the diode conducts easily in only one direction
Assumes the whole supply drives current through the resistor; the reverse-biased diode blocks it
Swaps the bias effect; reverse bias raises the barrier and widens the depletion region

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: p-n Junction Diode: Depletion Region, Barrier Potential, and Forward/Reverse Bias
questions.question: The reverse voltage on a diode is increased from 5 V to 10 V, both values being well below its breakdown voltage. The reverse current:
questions.explanation:
The reverse current is limited by how many minority carriers are thermally generated, not by the applied voltage.

Even a small reverse voltage sweeps all of them across, so the current saturates and stays nearly constant until breakdown.
questions.hint: Why is it called the reverse saturation current?
distractor_logic: Treats the diode as an ohmic resistor; reverse current saturates and hardly changes with voltage
Reverse current does not fall as reverse voltage rises
The current direction is fixed by the bias polarity, which has not been reversed

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: p-n Junction Diode: Depletion Region, Barrier Potential, and Forward/Reverse Bias
questions.question: The temperature of a reverse-biased silicon diode is raised considerably. Its reverse current:
questions.explanation:
Higher temperature generates more electron-hole pairs across the band gap.

This raises the minority-carrier concentration, so the reverse current increases sharply with temperature.
questions.hint: Minority carriers come from thermal generation.
distractor_logic: Heating produces more electron-hole pairs, so the current cannot fall
Ignores the strong temperature dependence of minority-carrier generation
Direction is set by the bias polarity, not by temperature

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: p-n Junction Diode: Depletion Region, Barrier Potential, and Forward/Reverse Bias
questions.question: A silicon diode (barrier about 0.7 V) and a germanium diode (barrier about 0.3 V) are each connected in forward bias, and the applied voltage is slowly raised from zero. Which begins to conduct appreciably first?
options: The silicon diode, at about 0.7 V
The germanium diode, at about 0.3 V
Both together, at the same voltage
Neither, until the voltage reaches 1.1 V
questions.explanation:
A diode conducts appreciably once the forward voltage exceeds its barrier (knee) voltage.

Germanium's barrier of about 0.3 V is reached before silicon's 0.7 V, so the germanium diode conducts first.
questions.hint: The smaller barrier is overcome sooner.
distractor_logic: Silicon needs the larger forward voltage, so it starts later
The two barrier potentials differ, so the knee voltages differ
Confuses silicon's band gap of 1.1 eV with a forward knee voltage

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: p-n Junction Diode: Depletion Region, Barrier Potential, and Forward/Reverse Bias
questions.question: Beyond the knee voltage, the forward current of a diode rises very sharply with voltage because:
options: the depletion region becomes wider and stores more charge
minority carriers are suddenly produced in large numbers by the field
the barrier is largely overcome, so majority carriers diffuse across the junction in large numbers
questions.explanation:
Once the applied voltage exceeds the barrier potential, the barrier offers little opposition.

The large number of majority carriers can then diffuse across, so the current grows rapidly with small increases in voltage.
questions.hint: Which carriers are plentiful, and what was stopping them before?
distractor_logic: Forward bias narrows the depletion region; widening happens only in reverse bias
Forward current is carried by majority carriers, not minority carriers
Breakdown occurs only under a large reverse bias, not in forward bias

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: p-n Junction Diode: Depletion Region, Barrier Potential, and Forward/Reverse Bias
questions.question: In the depletion region of an unbiased p-n junction, the direction of the built-in electric field is:
options: from the p-side to the n-side
zero, since the region has no free charges
from the n-side to the p-side
questions.explanation:
Positive donor ions are left on the n-side and negative acceptor ions on the p-side.

An electric field points from positive to negative charge, so it points from the n-side to the p-side and opposes further diffusion.
questions.hint: Find where the positive ions sit.
distractor_logic: Reverses the field; the positive ions are on the n-side, so the field points away from them
The field is set up by layers of charge on either side of the junction, so it is perpendicular to it
The region lacks free carriers but contains fixed ions, which produce a field

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Diode Applications: Rectifiers, and Zener, LED, Photodiode, and Solar Cell Devices
questions.question: A bridge rectifier is supplied with a 60 Hz AC input. The ripple frequency of its output is:
questions.explanation:
A bridge rectifier is a full-wave rectifier, so both half-cycles produce an output pulse.

Two pulses per input cycle means the ripple frequency is \( 2\times60=120 \) Hz.
questions.hint: How many output pulses per input cycle in full-wave rectification?
distractor_logic: Equal to the input frequency is the half-wave result; a bridge is a full-wave rectifier
Halving the frequency has no basis, since both half-cycles produce an output pulse
Doubles the frequency twice; the four diodes act in pairs, giving two pulses per cycle

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Diode Applications: Rectifiers, and Zener, LED, Photodiode, and Solar Cell Devices
questions.question: A Zener diode of breakdown voltage 10 V is connected in reverse bias in series with a 250 \( \Omega \) resistor across a 15 V supply, with no load. The current through the Zener is:
questions.explanation:
The Zener holds 10 V, so the resistor has \( 15-10=5 \) V across it.

\( I=5/250=0.02 \) A, which is 20 mA. With no load, all of this flows through the Zener.
questions.hint: Find the voltage across the series resistor first.
distractor_logic: Divides the full supply voltage by the resistance, ignoring the 10 V held across the Zener
Divides the Zener voltage by the resistance instead of the voltage across the resistor
Assumes a reverse-biased Zener blocks current; it conducts once the supply exceeds its breakdown voltage

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Diode Applications: Rectifiers, and Zener, LED, Photodiode, and Solar Cell Devices
questions.question: An LED is made from a semiconductor of band gap 2 eV. Taking \( hc=1240 \) eV nm, the wavelength of light it emits is about:
questions.explanation:
The photon energy is about equal to the band gap: \( E=hc/\lambda \).

\( \lambda=1240/2=620 \) nm, which is red light.
questions.hint: \( \lambda=hc/E \).
distractor_logic: Divides 1240 by 4 instead of 2
Forgets to divide by the band gap and just uses \( hc \)
Multiplies by the band gap instead of dividing

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Diode Applications: Rectifiers, and Zener, LED, Photodiode, and Solar Cell Devices
questions.question: A photodiode is operated in reverse bias rather than forward bias because:
options: in reverse bias the photodiode emits light, which is then measured
reverse bias makes the depletion region disappear, letting light pass
in forward bias no current can flow at all
in reverse bias the light-induced change in current is a large fraction of the small reverse current, so it is easy to detect
questions.explanation:
Light mainly changes the number of minority carriers.

In reverse bias the current is carried by minority carriers and is small, so a light-induced increase is a large fractional change.

In forward bias the large majority current would hide this change.
questions.hint: Think in terms of fractional change in current.
distractor_logic: Emitting light is the LED's function under forward bias, not the photodiode's
Reverse bias widens the depletion region; it does not make it disappear
A forward-biased diode conducts a large current; that large current is why the light effect is hard to notice there

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Diode Applications: Rectifiers, and Zener, LED, Photodiode, and Solar Cell Devices
questions.question: How many diodes are used in a bridge rectifier?
questions.explanation:
A bridge rectifier uses four diodes arranged so that two conduct in each half-cycle.

This gives full-wave rectification without needing a centre-tapped transformer.
questions.hint: Two diodes conduct in each half-cycle, and the pair changes every half-cycle.
distractor_logic: One diode makes a half-wave rectifier
Two diodes with a centre-tapped transformer make the other full-wave design, not the bridge
Six diodes are not used in the standard single-phase bridge

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Diode Applications: Rectifiers, and Zener, LED, Photodiode, and Solar Cell Devices
questions.question: Semiconductors chosen for solar cells ideally have a band gap of about 1.5 eV because:
options: a gap greater than 3 eV would absorb more sunlight
this gap is close to the energy of a large part of the photons in sunlight, so most of them can create electron-hole pairs
a gap near zero produces the largest voltage
the band gap has no effect on how much sunlight is absorbed
questions.explanation:
A photon can create an electron-hole pair only if its energy exceeds the band gap.

A gap near 1.5 eV lets most solar photons do this while still giving a useful voltage, so it is the best compromise.
questions.hint: Too large a gap wastes photons; too small a gap wastes voltage.
distractor_logic: Photons with energy below a large gap cannot create pairs, so an insulator-sized gap wastes most sunlight
A near-zero gap would give only a tiny voltage and behave almost like a conductor
Only photons with energy greater than the gap create electron-hole pairs, so the gap matters directly

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Diode Applications: Rectifiers, and Zener, LED, Photodiode, and Solar Cell Devices
questions.question: An ordinary p-n junction diode is generally NOT used in place of a Zener diode for voltage regulation because:
options: an ordinary diode cannot conduct in forward bias
Zener regulation works in forward bias, which an ordinary diode cannot do
its reverse breakdown is not sharp and it can be damaged in breakdown, whereas a Zener is specially doped for sharp, safe breakdown
an ordinary diode has no depletion region
questions.explanation:
A Zener diode is heavily doped, giving a very thin depletion region and a sharp breakdown at a well-defined voltage that it can survive.

An ordinary diode is not designed for this, so its breakdown is less sharp and can destroy it.
questions.hint: What special design feature does a Zener have?
distractor_logic: Ordinary diodes conduct well in forward bias; that is how they work as rectifiers
Swaps the operating mode; Zener regulation uses reverse breakdown
Every p-n junction has a depletion region

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Diode Applications: Rectifiers, and Zener, LED, Photodiode, and Solar Cell Devices
questions.question: An LED is required to emit light of wavelength 500 nm. Taking \( hc=1240 \) eV nm, the band gap of the semiconductor used should be about:
questions.hint: Divide 1240 by the wavelength in nm.
distractor_logic: Uses 1000 nm in place of 500 nm, halving the energy
Doubles the energy, as if the wavelength were 250 nm
A decimal-place slip, as if the wavelength were 5000 nm

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Bipolar Junction Transistor: Structure, Transistor Action, and Current Relations
questions.question: In a transistor, the emitter current is 10 mA and the collector current is 9.8 mA. The base current is:
questions.hint: Use \( I_E=I_B+I_C \).
distractor_logic: Confuses the ratio \( I_C/I_E=0.98 \) with a current value
Adds the currents instead of subtracting, as if \( I_B=I_E+I_C \)
Takes the emitter current itself as the base current

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Bipolar Junction Transistor: Structure, Transistor Action, and Current Relations
questions.question: A transistor has a common-base current gain \( \alpha=0.98 \). Its common-emitter current gain \( \beta \) is:
questions.explanation:
\( \beta=\dfrac{\alpha}{1-\alpha} \).

\( \beta=0.98/0.02=49 \).
questions.hint: Use \( \beta=\alpha/(1-\alpha) \).
distractor_logic: Slips a decimal place; \( \beta \) must be greater than 1
Uses \( 1/(1-\alpha) \) and forgets the factor \( \alpha \) in the numerator
Takes \( \beta \) equal to \( \alpha \), but the two gains belong to different configurations

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Bipolar Junction Transistor: Structure, Transistor Action, and Current Relations
questions.question: A transistor has \( \beta=99 \). If the base current is 20 \( \mu \)A, the collector current is:
questions.hint: \( I_C=\beta I_B \).
distractor_logic: This is the emitter current, \( I_B+I_C \), not the collector current
A factor-of-ten slip in the unit conversion from microamperes to milliamperes
Divides \( I_B \) by a factor instead of multiplying by \( \beta \)

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Bipolar Junction Transistor: Structure, Transistor Action, and Current Relations
questions.question: In a transistor, \( I_B=0.05 \) mA and \( I_C=2.45 \) mA. The common-base current gain \( \alpha \) is:
questions.hint: Find \( I_E \) first.
distractor_logic: 49 is \( \beta=I_C/I_B \), not \( \alpha \)
Inverts \( I_C/I_E \); \( \alpha \) can never exceed 1
Computes \( I_B/I_E \), the fraction lost to the base

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Bipolar Junction Transistor: Structure, Transistor Action, and Current Relations
questions.question: The collector current of a transistor is nearly equal to its emitter current. This is mainly because:
options: the base is thin and lightly doped, so very few injected carriers recombine there
the collector is the most heavily doped region
the base is thick, giving carriers time to reach the collector
the emitter-base junction is reverse biased
questions.explanation:
Carriers injected from the emitter must cross the base.

Since the base is thin and has few majority carriers to recombine with, about 95 to 99 percent of the carriers reach the collector, so \( I_C \) is almost equal to \( I_E \).
questions.hint: What would make carriers get lost on the way?
distractor_logic: The emitter, not the collector, is the most heavily doped region
A thick base would increase recombination, making \( I_C \) smaller
In normal operation the emitter-base junction is forward biased

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Bipolar Junction Transistor: Structure, Transistor Action, and Current Relations
questions.question: In an n-p-n transistor working in the active region, the charge carriers injected from the emitter into the base are:
options: holes, the majority carriers of the n-type emitter
electrons, the majority carriers of the n-type emitter
holes, the majority carriers of the p-type base
electrons, the minority carriers of the n-type emitter
questions.explanation:
The emitter of an n-p-n transistor is n-type, so its majority carriers are electrons.

With the emitter-base junction forward biased, these electrons are injected into the p-type base, where they are minority carriers, and most go on to the collector.
questions.hint: The emitter's own type decides the carrier.
distractor_logic: Holes are the minority carriers in n-type material
Carriers are injected from the emitter, not from the base
Electrons are the majority, not minority, carriers in an n-type emitter

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Bipolar Junction Transistor: Structure, Transistor Action, and Current Relations
questions.question: A transistor has \( \beta=24 \). Its common-base current gain \( \alpha \) is:
questions.explanation:
\( \alpha=\dfrac{\beta}{1+\beta} \).

\( \alpha=24/25=0.96 \).
questions.hint: Rearrange \( \beta=\alpha/(1-\alpha) \) for \( \alpha \).
distractor_logic: Gives \( 1+\beta \) instead of \( \beta/(1+\beta) \)
Gives \( 1/(1+\beta) \), which is \( I_B/I_E \), not \( \alpha \)
Adds \( 1/(1+\beta) \) to 1, giving a value above 1, which \( \alpha \) can never have

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Bipolar Junction Transistor: Structure, Transistor Action, and Current Relations
questions.question: The input characteristic of a transistor in common-emitter configuration is a graph of:
options: \( I_C \) against \( V_{CE} \), with \( I_B \) kept constant
\( I_C \) against \( I_B \), with \( V_{BE} \) kept constant
\( I_E \) against \( V_{CE} \), with \( I_C \) kept constant
\( I_B \) against \( V_{BE} \), with \( V_{CE} \) kept constant
questions.explanation:
In common-emitter mode, the input circuit is between base and emitter.

So the input characteristic plots base current \( I_B \) against base-emitter voltage \( V_{BE} \), with the output voltage \( V_{CE} \) held fixed.
questions.hint: Input side means base-emitter quantities.
distractor_logic: This is the output characteristic
This is a transfer characteristic, not the input characteristic
Uses the emitter current and holds the wrong variable constant; neither is part of the CE input characteristic

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Transistor as an Amplifier and Switch, and Digital Electronics: Logic Gates
questions.question: For a two-input NAND gate, which input combination gives output 0?
questions.explanation:
NAND is \( Y=\overline{A\cdot B} \).

\( A\cdot B=1 \) only when both inputs are 1, so NAND gives 0 only for \( A=1,B=1 \).
questions.hint: NAND is 0 exactly where AND is 1.
distractor_logic: Both inputs 0 gives \( A\cdot B=0 \), so NAND gives 1
With \( A=0 \), the product \( A\cdot B \) is 0 whatever \( B \) is, so NAND gives 1
With \( B=0 \), the product \( A\cdot B \) is 0 whatever \( A \) is, so NAND gives 1

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Transistor as an Amplifier and Switch, and Digital Electronics: Logic Gates
questions.question: A common-emitter amplifier uses a transistor with \( \beta=100 \), a collector resistance \( R_C=2 \) k\( \Omega \) and an input resistance \( R_{in}=1 \) k\( \Omega \). Using \( A_v=-\beta\left(\dfrac{R_C}{R_{in}}\right) \), the voltage gain has magnitude:
options: 200, with the output in phase with the input
200, with the output \( 180^\circ \) out of phase with the input
50, with the output \( 180^\circ \) out of phase with the input
2, with the output \( 180^\circ \) out of phase with the input
questions.explanation:
\( |A_v|=\beta R_C/R_{in}=100\times2/1=200 \).

The negative sign shows the output is inverted, that is, \( 180^\circ \) out of phase.
questions.hint: Keep track of both the size and the sign of the gain.
distractor_logic: The magnitude is right but the minus sign means inversion, not an in-phase output
Inverts the resistance ratio, using \( R_{in}/R_C \)
Uses only the resistance ratio and forgets the factor \( \beta \)

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Transistor as an Amplifier and Switch, and Digital Electronics: Logic Gates
questions.question: The two inputs of a NAND gate are joined together and fed a single input \( A \). The gate now behaves as:
questions.explanation:
With both inputs equal to \( A \), the output is \( \overline{A\cdot A} \).

Since \( A\cdot A=A \), this becomes \( Y=\overline{A} \), a NOT gate.
questions.hint: Replace \( B \) by \( A \) in \( \overline{A\cdot B} \).
distractor_logic: Forgets the inversion built into NAND
No OR behaviour arises from joining the inputs of a NAND
Ignores the inversion; \( \overline{A\cdot A}=\overline{A} \), not \( A \)

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Transistor as an Amplifier and Switch, and Digital Electronics: Logic Gates
questions.question: The output of an AND gate is fed into a NOT gate. The Boolean expression for the final output is:
questions.explanation:
The AND gate gives \( A\cdot B \).

The NOT gate inverts the whole of this, so \( Y=\overline{A\cdot B} \), which is the NAND gate.
questions.hint: The bar covers everything that enters the NOT gate.
distractor_logic: This is OR followed by NOT (NOR), not AND followed by NOT
Inverts each input separately instead of inverting the whole AND output
Ignores the NOT gate

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Transistor as an Amplifier and Switch, and Digital Electronics: Logic Gates
questions.question: In the truth table of a two-input OR gate, how many of the four rows have output 1?
questions.explanation:
\( Y=A+B \) is 1 whenever at least one input is 1.

Rows 01, 10 and 11 give 1; only 00 gives 0. So 3 rows have output 1.
questions.hint: Find the only row where OR gives 0.
distractor_logic: Exactly one row with output 1 describes the AND gate
Undercounts; only the row with both inputs 0 gives 0
The row \( A=0,B=0 \) gives \( A+B=0 \), so not every row is 1

questions.chapter_name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.topic: Transistor as an Amplifier and Switch, and Digital Electronics: Logic Gates
questions.question: A transistor is used as a switch in common-emitter mode with supply \( V_{CC} \). When the input voltage is low (logic 0), the transistor is in:
options: saturation, and the output voltage is close to zero
cutoff, and the output voltage is high, close to \( V_{CC} \)
cutoff, and the output voltage is close to zero
the active region, and the output equals the input
questions.explanation:
A low input gives almost no base current, so the transistor is in cutoff and \( I_C\approx0 \).

With no current through \( R_C \), there is no voltage drop across it, so the output \( V_{CE}\approx V_{CC} \), which is high.
questions.hint: No collector current means no drop across \( R_C \).
distractor_logic: Saturation needs a high input voltage that drives a large base current
